text:
CITATION
:
Shalma v. Shalma, 2013 ONSC 2487

COURT
FILE NO.:
FS – 10 - 358390

DATE:
20130426

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

)

)

Grace Shalma

Applicant

– and –

Victor Shalma

Respondent

)

) )

) )

) )

) ))

Aurelio Pascuzzi, counsel for the Respondent

)

)

)

)

HEARD:
March 25, 26, 27, 28 and April 2, 2013

KITELEY J.

[
1
]

The issues in
this trial focused primarily on access, child support, and spousal support.

BACKGROUND

[
2
]

Ms. Shalma was
born in Japan in 1962 and is now 51 years old.   Mr. Shalma was born in Morocco
in 1948 and is now 64 years old. They met in 2000 when Ms. Shalma
rented an apartment in
Mr. Shalma’s house with her daughter Leah who was then 2 years old. They began
to live together early in 2001 at which time
Ms. Shalma was approximately 40 years old and Mr.
Shalma was approximately 53 years old.

Eric was born November 11, 2003 and is now 9.5 years old. The
parties married on April 1, 2004.

Ms. Shalma was not employed. Mr. Shalma was a
carpenter.  He also had an ownership interest in residential properties.

[
3
]

In December
2004, Ms. Shalma and her daughter were deported to South Korea. Mr. Shalma
cared for Eric and worked full time. Mr. Shalma made efforts to have Ms. Shalma
return to Toronto. In September 2006, he took Eric to Israel and arranged for
Ms. Shalma and her daughter to move to Israel to care for Eric while Mr. Shalma
returned to Toronto.  Ms. Shalma and Leah and Eric lived in Israel until June
2008 when Ms. Shalma and Leah were able to return to Toronto. The family lived together
in one of the houses Mr. Shalma owned.

[
4
]

On June 10,
2009, Ms. Shalma took Eric from school and left the matrimonial home without
notice to Mr. Shalma.  She initially lived in a shelter.

[
5
]

Mr. Shalma
started proceedings in the Ontario Court of Justice because of Ms. Shalma’s
disappearance with Eric. On August 17, 2009, Zuker J. made an order appointing
the OCL.  He also directed that Mr. Shalma would have access which consisted of
the first three weekends of every month from Fridays after school to Mondays at
the commencement of school with pick up and drop off at McDonald’s. On
September 9, 2009, Sherr J. made an order giving Ms. Shalma temporary custody. He
ordered that Mr. Shalma would have Eric on three consecutive weekends out of
four from Fridays at school to Mondays at school.  He permitted Mr. Shalma to
take the child to synagogue.  On a without prejudice basis he directed Mr.
Shalma to pay child support of $462 per month commencing September 15, 2009 based
on imputed income of $50,000 annually.

[
6
]

In 2009, Mr.
Shalma issued an Application for divorce.  In that action, Ms. Shalma obtained
an ex parte order from Goodman J. dated October 22, 2009 restraining Mr. Shalma
from disposing of his interest in properties municipally known as 813, 815 and
817 Sheppard Ave. The motion was adjourned to November 5
th
.

[
7
]

On November 9,
2009, Zuker J. made an order effective July 1, 2009 directing Mr. Shalma to pay
spousal support of $2,000 per month and child support of $845 per month based
on imputed income of $96,000.

[
8
]

On November 19,
2009, Paisley J. continued the order restraining Mr. Shalma from transferring
his interest in his three properties and on November 26, 2009, Czutrin J.
continued it as well.

[
9
]

In late 2009,
Ms. Shalma began a relationship with Tom Muffoletto.

[
10
]

In April 2010,
Mr. Shalma did not return Eric to his mother’s home and then refused to do so. He
said he kept him because he was trying to register him in a Jewish school and
he needed to wait until the principal was available. He said that Ms. Shalma
had disappeared with Eric in 2009 and he thought he could do what he wanted as
well.

[
11
]

In response, Ms.
Shalma issued an Application in this court and on April 26, 2010, she obtained
a restraining order as well as an order requiring Mr. Shalma to immediately
return Eric to his mother with police authorized to enforce the order.
Paisley J. stayed access pursuant to the order made by Sherr J.  On April 29,
2010, Paisley J. made a referral to the Office of Children
’
s Lawyer.

[
12
]

On April 30,
2010 Paisley J. issued a divorce judgment in the action that Mr. Shalma had
commenced.

[
13
]

On May 11, 2010,
Czutrin J. made an order for “temporary temporary access “every Saturday from
9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with exchanges at the Supervised Access Centre.   He
also made another referral to the Office of Children’s Lawyer.

[
14
]

The report of
the OCL pursuant to the April 29, 2010 order of Paisley J. is dated September
9, 2010. Pursuant to s. 30(9) of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
, that
report is admissible without the author being called as a witness. Ms. Shalma
relies on the recommendations contained in the report while Mr. Shalma is
strongly opposed to them.  I do note the concluding paragraph as follows:

Eric
was observed to have a strong, affectionate relationship with his mother, which
in the face of intense pressure to speak and act otherwise, strongly suggests
that the mother-son relationship is beneficial and intact.  However, there is
significant risk that the effect of continued negativity from his father could
erode Eric’s confidence in and love for his mother. Given Mr. Shalma’s lack of
respect for authority, he is not likely to obey a court order to refrain from
his negative comments.  Having Mr. Shalma’s access supervised and limited would
protect Eric somewhat from his father’s adverse influence.   Thus it is
recommended that Mr. Shalma have reduced access time and that all access be
supervised either at an access centre, a synagogue or by a supervisor approved
by the court.   While supervised access each week will represent a dramatic
change in Eric’s life, it appears necessary to address the alienation process
that has been ongoing since the separation. If Mr. Shalma wants to parent Eric
for longer periods outside of supervision, he should be assessed by a
registered psychologist to determine his ability to understand the effect of
his words and actions on Eric as well as his ability to make the changes
necessary to ensure Eric’s well-being.

[
15
]

And the recommendations
were as follows:

1.

Ms. Shalma to
have sole custody of Eric.

2.

All of Mr.
Shalma’s access to Eric to be supervised either at an access centre, a
synagogue or by someone approved by the court.

3.

All access
exchanges to be supervised by Access for Parents and Children.

4.

Eric to call his
father once a week on a Wednesday after school and, if there is no visit on the
weekend, also on the weekend.

[
16
]

On January 6,
2011, Paisley J. made an order that provided that Mr. Shalma would have two
hours of supervised access each week and he directed that the observation notes
be provided to the court.

[
17
]

Mr. Shalma had
transferred his interest in the three properties on Sheppard Ave. to Sheppard
Heights Developments Inc. On January 11, 2011, Sachs J. dismissed a motion by
Sheppard Heights Developments Inc. to set aside the order of Paisley J. dated
November 19, 2009 on the basis that she was not satisfied that Mr. Shalma had
forfeited his interest in the properties before the making of that order.

[
18
]

On March 3, 2011
Ms. Shalma obtained an ex parte order issuing a certificate of pending
litigation against the three properties on Sheppard Ave.

[
19
]

In July 2011,
Ms. Shalma amended her Application to seek relief including claims made against
Mr. Shalma’s interest in the three properties on Sheppard Ave.

[
20
]

On October 14,
2011, Greer J. held a settlement conference and trial management conference
because the trial was scheduled to begin November 28, 2011. Counsel for Sheppard
Heights participated. Greer J. was told that the properties were under power of
sale, that Sheppard Heights had negotiated a stand-still agreement, and that the
properties would be sold. On the basis that the proceeds would be paid into
court, the certificates of pending litigation were vacated.  Greer J. adjourned
the trial to March 26, 2012.

[
21
]

On March 21,
2012 at a case conference that included counsel for Sheppard Heights, a written
agreement was made between Ms. Shalma and Sheppard Heights and Mr. Shalma and
then was incorporated into a consent order by Herman J.  Pursuant to that
agreement and order, Sheppard Heights paid Ms. Shalma $300,000 and she released
any claims she had or may have had against Mr. Shalma for an equalization of
net family property and arrears of child support and arrears of spousal support
up to January 1, 2012 and the arrears as at January 1, 2012 were fixed at
zero.   The trial date was adjourned to October 1, 2012.

[
22
]

In her evidence,
Ms. Shalma said that of the $300,000, $200,000 was on account of her claim for an
equalization of net family property and $100,000 was on account of arrears of
child support and spousal support. She said that the arrears had accumulated at
the rate of $2,845 per month from July 1, 2009 until January 2012 and that
approximated $100,000. Mr. Shalma did not give evidence on the calculation but
in his submissions, Mr. Pascuzzi pointed out that his client did not agree that
a substantial portion of the payment should be attributed as an equalization
payment.

[
23
]

On July 17,
2012, Wilson J. made a consent order for unsupervised access every Saturday
from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with exchanges at the Supervised Access Centre. The
order directed both parents to refrain from making derogatory comments about
the other and prohibited both parents from allowing the child to watch R-rated
movies.

[
24
]

On August 23,
2012, Czutrin J. made an order for access from Saturday August 25 at 9:00 a.m.
to August 26
th
at 5:00 p.m. so that Mr. Shalma could take Eric to
Great Wolf Lodge.  Mr. Shalma said that he was unable to take advantage of that
order because of transportation issues.

[
25
]

On September 18,
2012, Greer J. adjourned the trial to March 25, 2012.

ANALYSIS

Credibility
of the parties

[
26
]

In his
submissions, counsel for Mr. Shalma took the position that the evidence of Ms.
Shalma was not credible or reliable on financial matters.

[
27
]

Ms. Shalma also
urged that I not accept Mr. Shalma’s evidence.

[
28
]

I agree with Mr.
Pascuzzi that when it comes to her financial situation, Ms. Shalma’s disclosure
left much to be desired and her circumstances are by no means transparent.
That will lead me to draw inferences as indicated below. Mr. Shalma insisted
that Ms. Shalma frequently gambled. She denied it. The credit card statements
which she produced indicate two transactions totaling $832 in the month of
February 2013. Her own credit card statement appears to corroborate his
evidence. Whether Ms. Shalma gambles has no impact on the issues with respect
to Eric but may have relevance to the spousal support claim she has made.

[
29
]

As for Mr.
Shalma, it is clear that he is very angry with Ms. Shalma for depriving him of
Eric and because she managed to secure $300,000 from Sheppard Heights while he
received nothing.  He almost lost control on Thursday March 28 and at the
beginning of the morning on Tuesday April 2
nd
.  He says he is sorry
for having kept Eric in April 2010 but he accepts no responsibility for having
breached a court order that required him to return Eric to his mother.    I
infer that he is sorry that his actions caused an interruption in his
relationship with Eric and then had such a longstanding impact on access. But
he shows no remorse.  He blames the judge for making the original order for
supervised access and the other judge for finding his income was $96,000.   He
blames the OCL for the recommendation of supervised access.

[
30
]

In her evidence,
Ms. Shalma said that Mr. Shalma had again tried to have her deported and in her
document brief she included a letter from Canada Border Services Agency dated
February 9, 2010 confirming that she had attended an interview on December 21,
2009 concerning the allegation of misrepresentation and its implications on her
status in Canada and that a decision had been made that no further action would
be taken at that time.  That letter corroborates her evidence and demonstrates
the lengths to which Mr. Shalma was prepared to go to eliminate her from
Canada.

[
31
]

Based on the
foregoing, that I must be guarded about accepting his evidence on issues affecting
his relationship with Eric. On the other hand, his financial disclosure is
apparently comprehensive, particularly since his income consists of ODSP and
CPP.

Custody
and Access of Eric

[
32
]

Mr. Shalma had
made a claim for sole custody of Eric.  However, at the outset of the trial,
his lawyer said that custody was not in issue, that a final order giving Ms.
Shalma custody was conceded, and that the real issue was unsupervised and
extended access.  In his evidence, Mr. Shalma was not consistent with that
position but I rely on the submissions of his counsel in his opening trial
statement and in his closing submissions.

[
33
]

Ms. Shalma
agrees that access need not be supervised. However, she urges that pick up and
drop off continue to be at the Supervised Access Centre.  Her concern is that
in the past, Mr. Shalma has used access contacts as an opportunity to abuse her
verbally and emotionally and the only reason that that behaviour stopped was
because of supervision at the beginning and the end of each visit. She urges
the continuation of the status quo until Eric is 14 years old, although she
would consider access for a week in the summer.

[
34
]

I am satisfied
that the beginning and end of access need not be at the Supervised Access
Centre for these reasons.

[
35
]

First, since the
September 2010 report of the OCL recommending supervised access, more than 2.5
years have elapsed. At the outset of supervised access, there were some
instances where Mr. Shalma was less than co-operative and respectful of the
restrictions. However, as the review of the supervisors’ notes from July, 2011
indicate, there have been no problems either during the two hour period of
supervised access which continued until July 2012, or at the beginning and end
of access since that time.  There have been 26 visits between July 2012 and
February 9, 2013 and on each occasion, Mr. Shalma was on time at the beginning
and at the end of the visit, there were no issues with staff, there were no
“critical incidents” and the supervisor observed affectionate behaviour between
Mr. Shalma and his son.

[
36
]

I understand Ms.
Shalma
’s
point that there have been no problems because the beginning and end of access
have been supervised. I also understand her concern based on Mr. Shalma’s
historical behaviour since his bitterness toward her was apparent during his
evidence, particularly when she cross-examined him.  I am mindful of the
observation of the OCL that Mr. Shalma demonstrated a lack of respect for
authority which was demonstrated by his loss of control twice during the trial.
However, I am satisfied that Mr. Shalma has been persistently respectful of the
restrictions on him for almost two years from which I infer that even though he
continues to be very angry with her, he has learned that he must modify his
behaviour if he is to increase his access with Eric. Notwithstanding his
bitterness and resentment toward Ms. Shalma, and his failure to accept
responsibility for his past actions, he is highly motivated to have overnight
access and I am optimistic that he will be compliant with the order I make in
order to accomplish that objective.

[
37
]

Second, Ms.
Shalma lives in a condominium with controlled access and Eric is now 9.5 years
old and more mature than he was in September 2010 when the OCL made the
recommendation. The combination means that Mr. Shalma can drop off Eric at the
front door, Eric can enter the lobby, and Ms. Shalma can greet Eric in the
lobby. There will be no point when Eric is unsupervised and there will be no
point of contact between Mr. Shalma and Ms. Shalma.

[
38
]

Third, there are
limitations in dealing with the Supervised Access Centre which means that
access must occur on a rigid schedule when supervisors are available. In
addition, the S.A.C. closes for two weeks each summer. More flexibility is
required in order to provide more opportunities for Eric to see his father.

[
39
]

Being satisfied
that the beginning and the end of access need not be supervised, I turn to the
details of access.  As indicated above, the first order in the Ontario Court of
Justice established a regime of Mr. Shalma having the first three weekends of
every month and the second order directed that he would have Eric on three
consecutive weekends out of four.  The current order is every Saturday from
9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. At trial, Mr. Pascuzzi took the position that access
should be on alternate weekends from Friday from school to Sunday evening. Mr.
Shalma asked for every weekend but said that alternate weekends would be ok.
Mr. Shalma also said that after two months, the alternate weekends should end
on Monday morning at school. Indeed, Mr. Shalma said that after two months, he
wanted full custody.   Since that is inconsistent with the legal submissions by
his lawyer, I will not consider it.

[
40
]

I am mindful
that for two years, Mr. Shalma was the only parent in Toronto.   Mr. Shalma
took Eric to Israel but then resumed his role as parent in 2008 when Ms. Shalma
and Eric and Leah arrived. He has a long standing relationship with his son.
The supervisors’ notes of the beginning and end of access visits describe that
it is a loving relationship.  Ms. Shalma agreed that the relationship with his
father is important to Eric. Ms. Shalma also agreed in cross-examination that
overnights might start but she insisted that it would only be Saturday night
because the Supervised Access Centre is not available on Friday.  I am
satisfied that it is in Eric’s best interests that access be increased
substantially and include overnights.  Eric is entitled to have extended visits
with his father including over the summer.

[
41
]

However, I do
have two concerns. The first has to do with Eric’s homework. In
cross-examination, Ms. Shalma asked what would happen to Eric’s homework if he
was overnight with his father.  Mr. Shalma said that if he has homework, he
would skip the Thursday evening but then he wanted every weekend from Friday to
Sunday because it would not interfere with his homework. In submissions, Mr.
Pascuzzi said that his client would make sure that Eric gets the homework help
he needs, perhaps through his synagogue.

[
42
]

I have little
expectation that Mr. Shalma is able to help Eric with his homework. Mr. Shalma
does not have a plan to respond to Eric’s needs in that regard.   Bringing him
back on Monday means that it is likely he will not do his weekend homework.  Eric
already has homework assignments and that will increase over time.  If Eric
sees his father from Friday after school to Monday morning as requested by Mr.
Shalma, there is a real risk that his homework will not be done and Eric will
start the school week on the wrong foot. For that reason, generally during the
non-summer months, Eric should return early enough on Sunday to complete his
homework.

[
43
]

The second
concern has to do with how Mr. Shalma refers to Ms. Shalma when Eric is with
him.  In the report of the Office of Children’s Lawyer, this concern was
raised. I am mindful that the report contains hearsay. However, I had the
opportunity to observe Mr. Shalma throughout the almost five days of trial
including his evidence over parts of two days.  It is fair to say that he has
no respect for Ms. Shalma. For that reason, the longer the duration of the
visit, the more opportunity Mr. Shalma has to communicate that attitude to
Eric.  I infer from his evidence and his attitude towards her that he probably
has made offensive and derogatory comments to Eric about his mother. In
cross-examination, Ms. Shalma said that she fears Mr. Shalma continues to use
foul language against her because, while she does not have evidence, Eric
appears to have changed whenever she picks him up after a visit with his
father. She said that Mr. Shalma cannot control himself and pointed out the
recommendation contained in the report of the OCL that before such access
occurred, Mr. Shalma should be assessed to determine his ability to understand
the effect of his words and actions on Eric as well as his ability to make the
changes necessary to ensure Eric’s well-being.

[
44
]

Immediately
following the separation, it appears that each parent was making derogatory
comments about the other. I heard no evidence that Ms. Shalma continues to do so.
I will make an order directing Mr. Shalma not to do so. But his disrespectful
and derogatory attitude towards Ms. Shalma will also have an impact on the
duration of visits.

[
45
]

I will begin
overnights with the first visit for one night and then commence two nights.

[
46
]

Mr. Shalma also
asks for access every Thursday from after school to 6:00 or 7:00 p.m.   Every
Thursday may have an impact on homework and would be too close to the alternate
Fridays.  I agree that a Thursday visit in the week in which he does not have
alternate weekends is appropriate.

[
47
]

In the summer,
Mr. Shalma’s preference is that he be allowed eight weeks so that he can take
Eric to Israel.  But he suggested that he and Ms. Shalma alternate weeks
throughout the summer as an alternative. Ms. Shalma agrees that one week each
summer would be reasonable from Saturday to Saturday but she will choose which
week.

[
48
]

At this age and
stage of Eric’s life, summer access should be gradually increased. It stands to
reason that as Mr. Shalma is increasingly entitled to extended time with Eric,
that Ms. Shalma is also entitled to an equal amount of uninterrupted time
during the summer.

[
49
]

Mr. Shalma asked
for an extended visit during March break but did not provide the details of his
request. He has no proposals for what he would do with Eric.  If the week were
available, Ms. Shalma may have options.  I am not prepared to alternate March
break weeks but will extend the weekend visit as indicated below.

[
50
]

Mr. Shalma has
also asked for special events such as Father’s day and birthdays.   Ms. Shalma
did not respond to that request but I consider it fair to accommodate that
request so long as she has reciprocal time on Mother’s day and to alternate
Eric’s birthday.

[
51
]

Mr. Shalma has
also asked to have access for Jewish religious events including Yom Kippur,
Sukkot, Rosh Hashanah and Passover. Ms. Shalma agreed that he should have
access on one such occasion and that she would choose it.  I do not consider
that to be fair or workable. It is not just that Ms. Shalma should be able to
choose the religious events that Eric would be permitted to share with his
father. Mr. Shalma was not specific about the times on such occasions that he
requested. In cross-examination, he agreed to leave it to me. In an ideal world,
that is something the parents could work out. Unfortunately the two parents are
incapable of negotiating the dates.  I have set out expectations below as to
how this issue will be resolved.

[
52
]

Mr. Shalma does
not celebrate Christmas but he agrees that it is important to Ms. Shalma. Mr.
Shalma has asked that he have extended access each year with Eric from December
26
th
to January 1
st
. As a further option, Mr. Pascuzzi
suggested that the arrangement alternate from year to year so that in year 1,
Mr. Shalma have Eric from December 26 to December 30 and Ms. Shalma could have
New Year’s Eve and Day; and in year 2, Mr. Shalma would have Eric from December
26 to the day before school.  The school break in December is generally for two
weeks but the proximity between the end of school and December 25
th

changes from year to year. Ms. Shalma resisted an extended visit in December
because she said she had many things scheduled and she said that Mr. Muffoletto
has a cottage in the United States and she has to go there with him. I would
have preferred more details about the location of the cottage and the extent to
which they expect to visit it in December.  However, to enable Mr. Shalma and
Eric to spend time together during that school break, to ensure that Ms. Shalma
always has Eric on Christmas Day, and to give her equal extended time, I will
establish the December access as December 26
th
to January 1
st
.

[
53
]

Mr. Shalma has
asked for access to teachers, doctors and dentists.  Ms. Shalma is not opposed
to him having access to information about Eric but she is concerned that he not
be permitted to make medical decisions, such as vaccinations.  I agree that
that is a reasonable concern.

[
54
]

Neither parent
raised an issue about Eric’s passport. In response to my question, Ms. Shalma
said that she had Eric’s Canadian passport but it had expired.  She also has
Eric’s Israeli passport and she was not sure if it had expired.  Since she has
custody of Eric, she should be the only person authorized to obtain passports.
Mr. Shalma did agree that he would not take Eric to another country without
consent of Ms. Shalma or a court order permitting him to do so.

[
55
]

Mr. Shalma has
asked for some of the long weekends such as Thanksgiving. To incorporate those
events would unduly complicate the schedule.   If a long weekend falls on his
regular access weekend, then Mr. Shalma will have an extended visit but I will
not incorporate special events such as that.

[
56
]

As indicated
below, I have been very detailed about the arrangements for Eric and his father
to be together. Such detail is required because the parents are incapable of
having a civilized conversation on the topic and cannot negotiate fine details
as most other parents can do. I have created a specific schedule but I cannot
anticipate every nuance. I expect the parents to apply the scheme set out below
to respond to unanticipated events. I strongly encourage the parents to find a
way to negotiate on an annual basis so that each can enjoy more flexibility
than what the following order will allow.

Restraining
order

[
57
]

Ms. Shalma is
adamant that the restraining order remain in place, particularly if access does
not begin and end at the Supervised Access Centre.  Mr. Pascuzzi takes the
position that the restraining order should be terminated and replaced with an
order that neither parent would harass the other.

[
58
]

Based on how Mr.
Shalma acted during the trial, I agree that Ms. Shalma is entitled to know that
Mr. Shalma’s behaviour will be subject to legal restrictions and accordingly,
the restraining order should continue. However, there needs to be exceptions to
accommodate access.

[
59
]

The restraining
order prohibits Mr. Shalma from directly or indirectly communicating with Ms.
Shalma. As a consequence, he has not been able to have telephone communication
with Eric. Ms. Shalma is not opposed to telephone contact  with Eric and
suggested the phone number of her condominium and accordingly, another
exception will be required.

Child
Support and Spousal Support

[
60
]

Ms. Shalma asks
for child support and relies on the order made by Zuker J. dated November 9,
2009 that Mr. Shalma’s income should be imputed to be $96,000. Mr. Shalma
resists paying child support on the basis of hardship.

[
61
]

Ms. Shalma is
not asking for ongoing spousal support. She does however ask for enforcement of
the arrears from February 1, 2012 to April 2013 pursuant to the order of Zuker
J. dated November 9, 2009 which arrears total approximately $40,000.

[
62
]

In his Answer
dated July 31, 2012, Mr. Shalma asked for spousal support in the amount of $750
per month retroactive to December 2004. In his closing submissions, Mr.
Pascuzzi continued to make that request.  He asks that the court impute income
of $30,000 to $35,000 to Ms. Shalma.

[
63
]

Neither party
made submissions as to whether the spousal support claims were pursuant to the
Family
Law Act
or the
Divorce Act
.
The parties have been divorced since
April 2010. The order made by Zuker J. in the Ontario Court of Justice was
pursuant to the
Family Law Act
.  Ms. Shalma is not asking to vary that
order. She seeks to enforce that order which means that she must establish that
she has been entitled to receive spousal support from February 1, 2012 to the
date of the trial.  Mr. Shalma asks that his obligation to pay spousal support
terminate as of February 1, 2012 which means that he seeks in the Superior
Court to vary an order of the Ontario Court of Justice.

[
64
]

It is
questionable whether the Superior Court has the jurisdiction to terminate an
order made by a judge of the Ontario Court of Justice. This jurisdictional
dilemma only arises because we do not have the benefit of a Unified Family Court
in Toronto.  In my view, it would be a travesty of justice to require these
parties to return to the Ontario Court to address the enforceability of the
order of Justice Zuker. It would be equally unjust to address Mr. Shalma’s
fresh claim for spousal support but send the claim to enforce the existing spousal
support order back to the Ontario Court of Justice. I do have jurisdiction to determine
whether Ms. Shalma is entitled to spousal support and I have jurisdiction over
the Family Responsibility Office.

[
65
]

As for the claim
by Mr. Shalma for spousal support, I intend to consider it pursuant to the
Family
Law Act
so that the claims by Ms. Shalma and by Mr. Shalma are on the same
legal foundation.  Having said that, I doubt that the outcome with respect to
their claims would differ if the analysis were pursuant to the
Family Law
Act
.

A.

Spousal
support for Ms. Shalma

[
66
]

A court may make
an order for spousal support in favour of a dependent. I turn to whether Ms.
Shalma has established that she has continued to be a dependent since January
1, 2012 when the arrears of spousal support were, on consent, reduced to zero.

[
67
]

Ms. Shalma had
sworn a financial statement dated March 18, 2013 to which she referred in her
examination-in-chief.  As a result of my questions to her, she prepared another
financial statement sworn March 26, 2013.

[
68
]

In that
statement and in her evidence, Ms. Shalma said that after being on social
assistance for over three years, in the spring of 2012, she used the funds paid
to her by Sheppard Heights to purchase a condominium in which she resides with
Eric and Leah.  As was apparent in cross-examination, there was a lack of
detail as to what she had done with all of the $300,000.   She owns the
condominium and a vehicle that she valued at $25,000. She has debts.  She is
engaged to marry Mr. Muffoletto.

[
69
]

She says she is
self-employed and works part-time earning gross income of $1,500 per month and
net income of $800 per month.  She did not provide any documents or information
to indicate her hours of work, her gross income or her expenses.  She said she
sells on-line bicycle parts for Gallery Cycle (a company that Mr. Muffoletto
owns) and she sells oil paintings in the company that belongs to her. She says
that she has been unable to update that company’s website for the last three
years because the court proceedings meant that she could not devote herself to
work. Ms. Shalma has a fine arts degree which she obtained before she came to
Canada in 1999.  She also receives child tax benefits for two children in the
amount of $735 per month. She has received unpredictable support which she
estimated at $100 per month leaving her with a total net income of $1,635 per
month or $19,620 annually. Ms. Shalma listed monthly expenditures of $2,470
leading to a deficit of $935 per month which she said was covered by increasing
her debt.

[
70
]

In response to
my question, Ms. Shalma produced her Notices of Assessment which indicate line
150 income as follows:   2009 -  $8,080; 2010 - $11,552; 2011 - $11,672.  She
said that last year her gross income was $18,420.

[
71
]

In her
financial statement, Ms. Shalma swore that the value of her condominium was
$200,000 and the value of her Mitsubishi was $25,000. According to the
statement, her bank account contained $570. She claimed an amount owing to her
by Mr. Shalma on account of child support and spousal support arrears from
February 1, 2012 In the amount of $44,324. She provided a Mastercard statement
dated March 16, 2013 with a balance owing of $2,613.  She provided a statement
from her CIBC Visa account for the period ending February 25, 2013 showing a
balance of $7,425 including cash advances in the preceding month of $1,416. She
provided a statement from her CIBC Visa Infinite Card for the period ending
January 27, 2013 which showed a balance due of $5,395 including cash advances
that month totaling $1,600. The payment made that month was in the amount of $1,500.
She provided a statement from her TD Visa statement dated March 7, 2013 which
showed a balance of $3,954. This statement included an expenditure of $520 and
$312 on February 7 and 12, 2013 respectively to Woodbine Gaming North Toronto.
The payment made on March 25
th
on the outstanding balance was only
$100.  Ms. Shalma has a line of credit with the TD Bank. As of January 31,
2013, the balance owing was $13,287.  She made nine cash withdrawals in January
that totaled $2,900.  She made one payment on January 14, 2013 in the amount of
$500. On her Mastercard, the statement dated February 15, 2013 indicated that
Ms. Shalma owed $5,213. Ms. Shalma produced the conditional sales contract for
the Mitsubishi which indicated that it was purchased in June 2012 and she owed
at that time approximately $16,000.   She makes monthly payments of $241.36.

[
72
]

In
cross-examination, Mr. Pascuzzi took Ms. Shalma to her bank statements and
demonstrated that she was unable to account for what she had done with the
$300,000.  He also demonstrated that her bank statements did not corroborate
her evidence in several respects including that there was no record of deposits
for the child tax benefit as a result of which he suggested that Ms. Shalma had
failed to disclose her bank accounts. Based on her lack of comprehensive
disclosure, Mr. Pascuzzi urged me to impute income to her of $30,000 to $35,000.

[
73
]

I accept that
Ms. Shalma has not fully disclosed her financial circumstances. Her evidence
about her bank accounts created more questions than answers. She was adamant
that she was not gambling, yet her credit card statement appears to corroborate
Mr. Shalma’s evidence that she did gamble.  I infer that her evidence on
financial matters might not be credible and reliable. However, on balance, based
on the credit card statements, I accept that she is managing her household by
increasing her credit card indebtedness and her credit line debt.  But that
does not mean she continued to be entitled to spousal support after January 1,
2012.

[
74
]

Ms. Shalma is
working for the person she intends to marry.  She has a fine arts degree from
Soeul.  Based on her organization of documents and her presentation of her
evidence and her cross-examination of Mr. Shalma, she appears quite clever. She
may be underemployed.   She is only working part-time and with both her children
in school and the legal proceedings  coming to an end, she should be able to
work full time.  Accepting all of that, I am not prepared to impute income to
her of $30,000 to $35,000 annually.

[
75
]

Ms. Shalma was
found to be entitled to spousal support pursuant to the temporary order made
November 9, 2009 and then she agreed that as of January 1, 2012, the arrears
were zero.  Since that time, she received $300,000, acquired the condominium
and the Mitsubishi.  She is working and has not provided sufficient disclosure
about her income. The relationship between Mr. Shalma and Ms. Shalma was
carried on from early 2001 to June 2009.  However, the total period of
cohabitation was from sometime in 2001 to December 2004 and from June 2008 to
June 2009.  Given that short period of time, the difference in the ages of Mr.
Shalma and Ms. Shalma, the income and assets that she has disclosed (which are
superior to that of Mr. Shalma), I am not persuaded that Ms. Shalma was
entitled in law to spousal support pursuant to the
Family Law Act
from
February 1, 2012 to the present and accordingly, the arrears should be
eliminated.

[
76
]

Mr. Shalma takes
issue with the amount he was ordered to pay pursuant to the order made November
9, 2009.  He was not represented at that time.  Zuker J. made a finding that
his income should be imputed to be $96,000. I was not given the evidence on
which Zuker J. relied but I understand from the evidence before me that it was
based on Mr. Shalma’s 2008 tax return arising from rental income from some or all
of the Sheppard Ave. properties.  During the trial, Ms. Shalma provided a copy
of pages 1 and 2 of Mr. Shalma’s 2008 tax return. His sources of income
included gross income at line 160 in the amount of $54,000 (which I assume was
rental income) and net income at line 126 in the amount of negative $73,195.
His line 150 income
for that year was a negative of $64,748. Based on the record before me, I
cannot make any observations about the appropriateness of the order made by
Zuker J.

B.

Spousal
support for Mr. Shalma

[
77
]

I turn to the
question as to whether Mr. Shalma is entitled to spousal support.  He must
establish that he is a dependent of Ms. Shalma.

[
78
]

Between 2001
(when they starting living together) and June 2009 (when they separated), it
appears from the evidence before me that Mr. Shalma was working as a carpenter
and he was managing the rental properties.  He said he had not been able to
continue to pay the mortgages on the Sheppard properties, part of which had
been incurred because he spent $50,000 to $60,000 to get Ms. Shalma and Leah
back in Canada.  He had transferred his interest in those properties to
Sheppard Heights and he became a 50% shareholder.  He left when he was evicted
by the Sheriff.  He appears bitter that Ms. Shalma managed to obtain $300,000
when he said he got nothing from the properties.   As indicated above, his 2008
income tax return disclosed substantial income which was likely rental income,
but a substantial loss.  I am satisfied that until June 2009, Mr. Shalma was
self-supporting and was not dependent on Ms. Shalma.

[
79
]

Mr. Shalma’s
2010 income tax return indicated his line 150 total income was $10,339.  In
2011, his line 150 income was $4,419. Mr. Shalma produced his T4A(P) for 2012
that indicated he received taxable CPP benefits of $2,027. He also produced his
T5007 for 2012 which indicated that he had received social assistance payments in
the amount of $15,001.

[
80
]

He produced a
letter from his doctor dated December 31, 2010 that he suffers from
spondylolysis in the lumbar area that had been progressively worsening; severe
chronic erosive gastritis-esophagitis; type 2 Diabetes Melitus; obesity due to
dietary indiscretion and lack of physical activity; dyslipidemia; increasing
arthralgia in both knees; fatigue/insomnia/and anxiety related to marital
problems and apparent financial problems. The doctor described the medications
he had prescribed and expressed his opinion that Mr. Shalma was unable to work
as a carpenter and that his ability to perform manual work was limited.  I was
not given any of the documentation that was relied on in order to obtain ODSP
but I am satisfied that he would not be in receipt of such funds had he not
established that he was disabled. I find that he is currently unemployable.

[
81
]

In November
2012, he moved to a rented apartment which has two bedrooms so that he can
accommodate Eric overnight.  His financial statement does not contain any
assets.

[
82
]

A statement from
Community and Social Services for the month of October 2011 indicates that he
received a total of $348.26 in that month. In November 2011, the total was $592
(plus arrears of $230.) It appears that ODSP began in late 2011 or early 2012.
The payment in the amount of $1,294 per month consisted of $590 for basic
needs, $474 for shelter, and $230 for special diet. Effective January 2013, the
amount increased to $1,305 per month consisting of basic needs of $596, shelter
of $479 and special diet of $230.  In addition, Mr. Shalma has been entitled to
approximately $170 per month from CPP, half of which appears to have been
seized by the Family Responsibility Office on account of arrears of spousal and
child support.

[
83
]

Mr. Shalma owns
a 2004 Chevrolet van which is parked because he cannot afford to drive it. When
he does drive, he borrows a car from a friend. He has a chequing account that
had a balance of $0.78. The pages from the passbook in 2012 indicate that the
main activity was the deposit of ODSP.

[
84
]

Just because Mr.
Shalma is unable to work and survives on public assistance does not mean that
he is entitled to spousal support. It is the case that Ms. Shalma’s standard of
living is better than his, but as she pointed out, for more than three years after
the separation in 2009, she was on social assistance. I am not persuaded that
he is a “dependent” within the meaning of the
Family Law Act
. Indeed, I
am satisfied that the claim for spousal support retroactively to December 2004
(which was the date that Ms. Shalma was deported) was asserted largely for
tactical reasons. There is no basis for such a claim.

C.

Child
Support

[
85
]

The original
order for child support was made pursuant to the
Family Law Act
.   I
continue to apply that legislation.

[
86
]

Mr. Shalma
acknowledges that he has a legal obligation to pay child support. His counsel
took the position that if support were ordered, it should be on the portion of
his ODSP that does not include the allocation in the amount of $230 for special
diet and therefor his income should be treated as $1,064 per month or $12,750 annually.

[
87
]

Counsel for Mr.
Shalma prepared a variety of divorcemate calculations based on assumptions of
his income at a low of $12,750 annually and a high of $15,500 annually.  His
calculations also assumed levels of income for Ms. Shalma in a range of $21,320
to a high of $35,000.  On those ranges, Mr. Shalma would be required to pay
child support in a range of $62 per month to a high of $212 per month. Counsel
for Mr. Shalma argued that no matter what the amount, Mr. Shalma should be
relieved of the obligation to pay child support based on hardship grounds.

[
88
]

I agree that for
purposes of child support, the special diet allocation should be ignored,
leaving Mr. Shalma with annual income of $12,750 plus an amount allocated to
Canada Pension.  It appears that he is entitled to receive $180 per month in
CPP but that half (or $84) is garnisheed on account of support and the other
half is deducted from his ODSP.  There is no evidence as to what will happen
with his CPP and OAS entitlement and his ODSP payments once he reaches age 65.

[
89
]

Mr. Shalma
functions at subsistence level.  He has health issues and is unemployable.   He
has no prospects of improving his standard of living which is lower than Ms.
Shalma
’s
standard of living.  I agree that this is a situation in which s. 10 of the
Child Support Guidelines applies and that I should award an amount that is
different than the amount determined according to the Guidelines because Mr.
Shalma would otherwise suffer undue hardship.

[
90
]

But that does
not mean he should be relieved of paying any child support. He has not voluntarily
paid any child support since the separation in June 2009. Modest amounts have
been garnisheed in recent months. He should be required to accept some
responsibility to reflect the principle that support for children is shared
between the parents. I will impose an ongoing obligation that reflects his
current circumstances.

[
91
]

I am also
satisfied that Mr. Shalma has no ability to pay the arrears of child support
and no prospect that his circumstances will change. There is no point in
retaining the arrears of child support accumulated after January 1, 2012
pursuant to the order of Zuker J.

[
92
]

Even though Mr.
Shalma appears to have limited means, his obligation to pay child support will
be binding on his estate.

Cost
of this proceeding

[
93
]

After the
parties have reviewed these reasons for decision and the order that follows, I
will hear submissions as to costs.
